Surviving COVID-19

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
What does it actually feel like to have COVID-19?
We’ve heard the numbers, the hard facts and that millions have it and hundreds of thousands are dying from it, but we’ve heard almost nothing from the people who have contracted the virus. I am proposing a character driven narrative about getting the virus with factual backing from a medical expert who can explain in layman terms how the virus works in the body

Summary:
Characters:

Kim
Kim contracted COVID in March while on a business trip in Germany. After returning to SA her children's school insisted she get tested, as she had recently traveled and had some symptoms. Once positive she self isolated with her husband and children. She has a great kinda upbeat look the whole experience. No-one in her family got tested, even though they had symptoms. Kim owns two hotels in JHB and CT, so once she recovered she decided that she needed to do something to help the fight against the virus and started an NGO called Ubuntubeds. She has about 700 hotels and B&B's offering free accommodation to field workers so they can be closer to hospitals.

Buli
Buli thinks she contracted the virus from a business associate from the USA. She was a lot sicker than Kim. She called it the "exhaustion disease" she couldn't get out of bed for over a week. She battled to breathe walking up and down her stairs. Her doctor prescribed antibiotics and flu meds. The flu meds seem to work she said, it could also have been that the virus had run its course naturally. She self-isolated with her son. I just spoke to her and she said he did leave the house to go shopping before they knew it was COVID, I will confirm again though. She is a little confusing.
An ambulance and the police arrived at her townhouse and said she needed to come with them, as the people in her complex were afraid
She is now starting an organisation (think tank) to help people going through being infected and how to get over it afterwards

Sivuyile Ntlanjana
Sivu works at the funeral parlour that worked on the funeral that has lit the fire that has spread the disease across Port st johns and the women prison in East-London .
I chatted to him briefly today, but I have a call with him in the am. He was extremely sick and hospitalised

Press Release:


Surviving COVID-19
Worldwide, countries are counting their dead and, with over 3 million confirmed global infections, the COVID-19 pandemic has the world in a stranglehold. Studies show that almost 80 percent of patients do pull through, most without any special medical intervention, proving that some bodies can fight back against the virus. Now meet some of the men and women who’ve battled the coronavirus and won.
Producer: Tarryn Crossman | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli


Script:









Time: 10:59

Macfarlane Moleli
Dr Kim Short
Buli Maliza
Sivuyile











 

Time code CHARACTER / VISUAL
1 00:00 VO Although Cape Town is now the epicentre of the virus with over 4000 infected and almost 50 percent of those recovered when Kim Whitaker returned to Cape Town in March after a business trip in Germany. There were hardly any infections.
2 00:15 KIM I went to go and fetch my kids from school and as I was packing I received a WhatsApp message from the school principal asking any parent who had been abroad or been to Europe to self quarantine. Either I could go and self quarantine by myself and be away from the family for two weeks or we could go into cell phone 10 together because I was already in the parking lot and I hadn't seen my kids in pretty much 10 days. I took the decision to pick them up rather and I'd rather be with them at home.
3 00:51 V/O At this point Kim had no fear of having the virus, As she had none of the required symptoms. She was simply following the school's protocol
4 00:59 KIM In a bit of rebellion I said No I'm going to get tested because I'm absolutely not positive. Quite late in the evening on Friday our doctor called and she told us over the phone listen Kim I'm so sorry but your tests come back positive and I think that was my surprise to find out that I wasn't back positive. And even in that short time we visited a café to go and fetch a coffee and then I visited a restaurant. We went and had supper like we sort of our normal routines and rituals. When the test came back positive I thought oh my gosh I have to call that restaurant in the red.
And the waiter has to go into self quarantine like this is terrible. I had to give them a list of everyone who had been into contact with. They confirmed my seat number on the airplane. They contacted everyone within a three meter radius sitting either behind me next to me etc. etc..

5 01:47 V/O Currently our team has over 1000 infections and close to 800 recoveries. But in March when Buli Malisa got tested the outbreak had just begun.
6 01:59 Buli It started with a cough, And Night Sweat. The cough was completely different from any other cough I've ever heard.
7 02:08 VO Maliza is an international businesswoman and even though she knew she was taking a risk in meeting overseas colleagues she was still in shock when she got a test results.
8 02:17 Maliza I think my doctor was more shocked than I was and I didn't know who was trying to come who we didn't know what to do. Eventually I jumped inside a car drove myself to the hospital. It's been probably about four or five hours. We tested the vitals and then they gave me an asthma pump for in case it develops. And when that happens then you'd call the hospital for the ambulance to come and pick you up.
9 02:43 Mac Link Doctor Kirsty Short is a biologist at the University of Queensland Australia. She's a viral pandemic specialist with dedicated her life's work to understanding the common flu. In all its mutated forms and is now applying that knowledge to cope in my team much more severe than the flu.
10 02:59 Dr Kirsty So you have a much higher chance of being hospitalised a much higher chance of potentially going into the ICU and a much higher chance of dying than if you got the flu. The big thing that we're noticing is its ability to cause what we call a cyclone storm. Well basically it means that it turns on the immune system which is normally a good thing but it doesn't tentacle your immune system starts coming out of control and it's going everything it can at this fast. But in the meantime we're in the background it's actually accidentally destroying the tissues in your lungs your lungs can then start to fill with fluid.

11 03:34 DR Kirsty As soon as you get fluid in your lungs you cooperate very well you can then get some damage to the cells that line your blood vessels. So what we see is that you can actually get problems with clotting so you have a situation where you've just got random clots forming your lungs aren't getting enough oxygen properly and that could cause other organs in your body to shut down as well.
12 03:53 VO On the 21st of March a funeral took place near Port St. John's in the Eastern Cape which resulted in close to 50 people being infected. Those 50 then traveled all over the province which contributed to a spike in the number of infections. Port St. John's is currently a red zone for cover 19 Sivuyile was the conductor of the funeral and on the 11th of April tested positive.
13 04:21 Sivuyile I was so worried about this disease, covid 19 because we heard that overseas there are hgigh numbers of deaths. I was worried about my life, I was worried about my sibnlings, at I'm the breadwinner, I thought if I go to hospital what are my siblings going to eat?
14 04:435 VO Sivuyile in a one bedroom house with his mom and four siblings. So he was unable to self isolated home and was admitted to St Barnabas Hospital in the Tron sky to complete his 14 days like.
15 04:58 Sivuyile I was the first perosn to be admitted at St Barnabas Hospital for Covid 19, so you can imagine they don't know what to a covid 19 patient is like. There is not TV in the ward, no radio – its just you. On day 3 when I woke up I had chest pains, I phoned one of the nurses, they didn’t have PPE clothing to protect themselves, so they couldn’t assist me when my condition deteriorated.; on the fourth day the PPE was delivered
16 05:36 VO after finding out she was positive Kim had to take extra precautions to protect her husband and children during isolation.
16 05:43 Kim So the first conversation that I had with the Western Cape health department they gave me a whole bunch of guidelines so for example I should take separate cutlery and crockery I should stay in a separate room. So really trying to just keep minimal contact even though we're staying in the same space
17 06:02 Mliza Covid 19 is a virus. It's an energy cell. So the first few days visited it once you done so you need to work against it. It means we need it forces you to sleep you do the opposite for
18 06:17 Kim the last five days I lost my sense of smell and taste absolutely completely. It was bizarre. And apparently that's one of the symptoms that's coming out more and more
19 06:29 Sivuyile Something that helped me survive was the support that I got from the CEO of the hospital and the nurses. That keeps you sane, even though people cant come closer to you thye can still support you
20 06:42 KIM I was a little bit concerned about our three year old. He has had sort of lung issues since birth.
21 06:51 Kids footage washing hands
22 06:54 KIM My husband had very very mild symptoms. And our kids were tired for a day or two which is very unusual for them. So we assume that they got a very mild case of coronavirus. They never got tested and I never got retested. They sort of ran quite short on tests because it was as the spikes were happening. I guess we'll never really know for sure until there's an antibody test.
23 07:14 VO This was back in early March. The government tests have you can see ramped up testing 20 fold according to the COVID 19 Advisory Committee. The private sector also has a host of places to easily get tested after revealing his status.
Sivuyile was alienated and stigmatized by his community.

24 07:34 Sivuyile They hated me, they insulted me. The way they treated me made me feel like I wasn’t human. No one wanted to come near me everybody was runnin away from, me. They are uneducted about this covid 19 seriously and our people are going to die.
25 07:56 VO But this level of harassment is not only taking place in the more rural areas of the Eastern Cape. Buli lives in an upmarket area of Johannesburg and her neighbors allegedly tried to have her forcibly removed from her complex in fear of being infected.
26 08:13 BULI The police were knocking on my door and the ambulance was outside and then when I ask why they were here and said some neighbors are concerned. So I refused to open. Eventually the police said OK they're going to come back with the warrant of arrest.
Then I lost it in the incident. I'm going to instruct them to withdraw. And he did.

27 08:35 Buli cellphone This is the time when we need to love each other not hate each other in such a manner
28 08:42 Voice over Buli, Sivuyile and Kim all managed to recover from the virus without meeting any medical intervention. And like them 80 per cent of people will recover from Covid 19. But according to Dr. Short contracting the virus doesn't guarantee you immunity.
29 08:59 Mac and Kim Mac: These people that say just like the common flu let's go out there. Let's get it let's build immunity against.

Kim: I mean it depends on how much of a gambler you are. The short answer is we don't know how long the immunity to this virus lasts for. And again that's because it's a new virus. I personally would not take that risk. But on top of that I would never forgive myself if I got infected and then I infected a vulnerable family member who succumb to the disease. Well our best hope is is that we'll be able to develop a vaccine. We already have several vaccine candidates that are in clinical trials. That's a really unprecedented speed at which that's happened.
Normally vaccines to get to that stage took five years. And I feel very optimistic that early next year we should see something coming out .
30 09:44 VO as most of the world sits in lockdown holding our breath for a vaccine around us life as we know it is changing. Whittaker owns a hub hotel called Once and after recovering from the virus. She wanted to do something to help the fight which gave birth to Ubuntu Beds.
31 10:04 KIM I was on a zoom call to Lombardy in Italy. And someone said to me what would you have done two weeks ago if you knew what you knew today? And. One of the entrepreneurs said I would have spoken to the hotels and I would have gotten them to accommodate the healthcare workers.
32 10:21 VO Ubuntu Beds has now close to 750 hotels and BNB’s offering free accommodation to frontline workers so they can safely isolate close to where they are on duty.

While in isolation Buli realized the need for professionals to work together against stigma and abuse And offer these skills to help needed to provide mental health support for a new business network. She founded that awoke Global Foundation.

33 10:51 Buli This is something that you cannot just leave to government to fight. You also need us as individuals to help to fight depended mic itself

We’ve heard the numbers, the hard facts and that millions have it and hundreds of thousands are dying from it, but we’ve heard almost nothing from the people who have contracted the virus. I am proposing a character driven narrative about getting the virus with factual backing from a medical expert who can explain in layman terms how the virus works in the body
metadata.Summary: Characters: Kim Kim contracted COVID in March while on a business trip in Germany. After returning to SA her children's school insisted she get tested, as she had recently traveled and had some symptoms. Once positive she self isolated with her husband and children. She has a great kinda upbeat look the whole experience. No-one in her family got tested, even though they had symptoms. Kim owns two hotels in JHB and CT, so once she recovered she decided that she needed to do something to help the fight against the virus and started an NGO called Ubuntubeds. She has about 700 hotels and B&B's offering free accommodation to field workers so they can be closer to hospitals. Buli Buli thinks she contracted the virus from a business associate from the USA. She was a lot sicker than Kim. She called it the "exhaustion disease" she couldn't get out of bed for over a week. She battled to breathe walking up and down her stairs. Her doctor prescribed antibiotics and flu meds. The flu meds seem to work she said, it could also have been that the virus had run its course naturally. She self-isolated with her son. I just spoke to her and she said he did leave the house to go shopping before they knew it was COVID, I will confirm again though. She is a little confusing.
